issues.legal_issue: Omitting facts about other accommodation from pleadings does not by itself defeat an otherwise proved bona fide claim for personal occupation.
material_facts: The landlord sought eviction for personal and family occupation and did not disclose in the plaint that her husband held a tenancy in another flat.
Her husband had left that flat years earlier, and his brother’s family had occupied it since then.

The trial court found that the landlord lacked suitable accommodation and bona fide required the premises; the Supreme Court held that the omission did not, by itself, show mala fides or disentitle her to relief.
issues.conclusion: The omission was not sufficient to disentitle the landlord from eviction relief where she otherwise proved her reasonable and bona fide requirement.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that an omission to plead facts about other accommodation is not, by itself, enough to defeat a claim if the landlord otherwise proves a bona fide requirement. The Court relied on the general approach in Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, including that the landlord is the best judge of residential requirements, and referred to Dinshaw Billimoria v. Rustomji Master and the cited Calcutta decisions on the nature of a landlord’s requirement. No separate statutory provision or earlier case was identified as governing the omission issue itself.

rule.if: residential_eviction_for_owner_use and omitted_spouse_rental and other_dwelling_occupied_by_another_household and personal_need_proved

predicates.residential_eviction_for_owner_use: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding seeking premises for personal or family occupation.
predicates.omitted_spouse_rental: The landlord did not plead that the spouse held a tenancy in another dwelling.
predicates.other_dwelling_occupied_by_another_house: The spouse had left that dwelling and another household was occupying it.
predicates.personal_need_proved: Evidence established the landlord’s reasonable and bona fide need for the premises sought.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks premises for personal use, omits a spouse’s rental accommodation that another household occupies, and proves the personal need, the omission alone does not disqualify the claim.

issues.legal_issue: Assessment of bona fide personal requirement must account for the actual legal security and practical suitability of alternative accommodation, rather than its theoretical availability.
material_facts: The landlord owned the premises sought and had no other premises of her own in the city.
Her husband’s use of one flat depended on a temporary licence from his employer, and he had no right to occupy it as a matter of course.
Another flat was occupied by the husband’s brother and family; it was a two-bedroom dwelling, and a partial eviction decree limited the husband’s entitlement to part of it.

The lower appellate court and High Court treated these dwellings as available based on the husband’s tenancy, possible future access, or continued possession, but the Supreme Court found that neither provided suitable and secure alternative accommodation in the circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The landlord proved her bona fide requirement; the alternative accommodation did not defeat her claim, and the eviction decree was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, the landlord is the best judge of residential requirements, and the court should not dictate how the landlord should live. The inquiry includes whether the landlord has a legal right to alternative accommodation and whether it is secure and suitable in practice. The Court also referred to Phiroze Bamanji Desai v. Chandrakant M. Patel concerning the precarious nature of a licensee’s possession, and to Dinshaw Billimoria v. Rustomji Master, Basant Lal Saha v. P.C. Chakravarty, and Ramendra Mohan Guha Sarkar v. Smt. Bedana Paul. The judgment did not identify a specific statutory provision governing this claim; the reference to proviso (f) of Section 11(1) of the Rent Control Act, 1948 appeared in its quotation from a cited Calcutta decision.

rule.if: residential_eviction_for_owner_use and claimant_owns_suit_premises and personal_need_proved and (alternative_use_is_temporary_permission or (alternative_is_occupied_by_another_household and usable_space_is_restricted))

predicates.residential_eviction_for_owner_use: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding seeking premises for personal or family occupation.
predicates.claimant_owns_suit_premises: The claimant owned the premises sought for occupation.
predicates.personal_need_proved: Evidence established the claimant’s reasonable and bona fide need for the premises sought.
predicates.alternative_use_is_temporary_permission: The claimant’s household used alternative accommodation only under a temporary permission that did not confer a secure right to occupy it.
predicates.alternative_is_occupied_by_another_house: Another household was occupying the alternative dwelling in fact.
predicates.usable_space_is_restricted: A limitation on the claimant household’s access to the alternative dwelling left only restricted space available.

issues.definition: When an owner proves a bona fide need for personal-use premises, temporary permission to use another dwelling or another household’s occupation combined with restricted usable space does not negate that need.
